title: The Main Structural Elements
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the main structural elements in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “The Main Structural Elements” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with the <header> element, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Meaningful structure and metadata make content easier to navigate, understand, share, and maintain across different devices and assistive technologies.

content_blocks.title: Semantic page structure
content_blocks.alt_text: Use native elements for their intended meaning and avoid adding unnecessary landmarks.
content_blocks.caption: Use this visual as a quick map; the sections below explain the decisions in more detail.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Meaningful structure and metadata make content easier to navigate, understand, share, and maintain across different devices and assistive technologies.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A header introduces a page or a section and can contain headings, logos, or navigation.

items.title: The <header> element
items.text: A header introduces a page or a section and can contain headings, logos, or navigation.

items.title: The <main> element
items.text: The main element identifies the dominant content of the page; use it for the primary unique content.

items.title: The <footer> element
items.text: A footer contains information about its nearest section or the page, such as authorship or related links.

items.title: The <nav> element
items.text: The nav element groups major navigation links. Not every set of links needs a nav landmark.

items.title: The <section> element
items.text: A section groups thematically related content and usually has a heading.

items.title: The <article> element
items.text: An article represents self-contained content that could make sense outside its current page context.

items.title: The <aside> element
items.text: An aside contains related but secondary content, such as a glossary or related links.

items.title: The <div> element
items.text: The <div> element is one of the decisions covered by The Main Structural Elements. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Create a small HTML example that demonstrates the main structural elements. Keep the markup minimal, give every element a clear purpose, and inspect the rendered result.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from The Main Structural Elements.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for the main structural elements.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: The page has meaningful header, navigation, main, article, and footer regions.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: The Main Structural Elements is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.

The <span> element is one of the decisions covered by The Main Structural Elements. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
